newsitem.title: USA: Motown Records CEO resigns, Polygram says.
newsitem.headline: Motown Records CEO resigns, Polygram says.

text.p: Andre Harrell, the flamboyant president and chief executive of soul music label Motown Records has resigned -- less than two years after he came to head the ailing company, Polygram Holding Inc. said Monday.
The announcement followed weeks of speculation about a restructuring at PolyGram's music operations. Late last week, sources said Harrell's reign had all but ended.
While the recruitment for a new Motown president is conducted, day-to-day operations at the legendary label will be overseen by its chairman, Clarence Avant, and Motown's senior staff, Polygram said.

Several music industry sources believe a restructuring will involve the promotion of Danny Goldberg, president of PolyGram's Mercury Records unit, to a broader role at PolyGram's U.S. music interests.
But music industry sources said final plans for Motown are still being discussed. Goldberg could not be reached for comment.

A PolyGram spokeswoman declined to comment on the speculation regarding Goldberg. However, she said there are no plans to change the structure of Motown in any substantial manner while the company recruits a new president.
PolyGram acquired Motown, which was founded in Detroit in 1959 by Berry Gordy Jr., in 1993.

In its heyday in the 1960s and 1970s, Motown helped launch the careers of the Jackson Five, the Supremes, the Temptations, Lionel Richie and the Commodores, Smokey Robinson & the Miracles, and the Four Tops. Their works are included in Motown's back catalogue of over 30,000 records.
But in recent years, Motown's presence on the cutting edge of black music has been minimal, as labels such as Death Row Records, Bad Boy Entertainment and Ruthless Records have taken up the slack.
The label's only current big seller is Boyz II Men, which hasn't released an album under Harrell's watch.

Industry sources said Harrell, who has been criticised for lavish spending habits and leading the legendary label toward sizeable losses, is leaving with a sizeable severance package because his multimillion-dollar five-year contract is being cut short.
Harrell joined in October 1995, having enjoyed much success with his own Uptown Records label.
Analysts have long noted that Polygram's music operations, not unlike many other record companies, are suffering from the dual problems of high overhead costs and sluggish sales.

"During 1996, the recorded-music industry started the painful process of pruning labels and staff as well as consolidating distribution operations, and we expect the industry will continue to be forced to cut overhead in order to maintain profitability," said John Penney, analyst with investment bank Sanford C. Bernstein & Co. Inc.
PolyGram also owns Island Records and A&M Records, neither of which has made much of an impact in the charts recently.
But Motown, which has seen its market share slide to under 1 percent of the total U.S. market in recent years, is considered the weakest link by far.

Goldberg has been credited with turning Mercury into one of PolyGram's crown jewels by signing such acts as the hit sibling trio Hanson. Other acts at Mercury include INXS, Carnie and Wendy Wilson and Lionel Richie, a former Motown star.
A spokeswoman for Goldberg would not return phone calls seeking comment on the changes at Motown.
Sources said they expect staff and artist cutbacks to occur at Motown as well.
Motown's current roster has over 25 artists, including Boyz II Men, which will release a new album this fall, Diana Ross, Stevie Wonder, Queen Latifah, Zhane, and the new group 98 Degrees.
"Changing top management can sometimes re-energise a label when market share is weak, although there's no assurance that it will," Penney said.
